topic: Station operation and test equipment (G4A, G4B; 26 pool questions)

notes.front: What does a notch filter do on an HF transceiver?
notes.back: It cuts out interference from a carrier that falls inside the receiver passband.
notes.explanation: It targets one unwanted carrier inside the band you are hearing, rather than noise pulses or splatter from elsewhere.
notes.example: A steady whistle from a carrier inside your SSB passband disappears when you tune the notch onto it.

notes.front: What does a noise blanker do?
notes.back: It reduces receiver gain briefly during each noise pulse.
notes.explanation: It acts in time rather than in frequency, so it only blanks the receiver while a pulse lasts.
notes.example: Ignition noise clicking on 40 m disappears when the blanker cuts gain for each brief pulse, leaving the SSB audio between them intact.

notes.front: What does a receiver's noise reduction control do, and what happens if it is turned up too far?
notes.back: It processes audio to reduce background noise; overdone, it can distort the received signal.
notes.explanation: Unlike a noise blanker's brief gain cut, noise reduction reshapes the audio continuously, so pushing it too hard changes the wanted signal too.
notes.example: Like an aggressive noise-cancelling filter on a voice recording: past a point it smears the voice as well as the hiss.

notes.front: What is plate current, in a vacuum-tube RF amplifier?
notes.back: The current flowing in the tube's plate circuit; its grid voltage regulates it.
notes.explanation: The tuning and loading controls of a tube amplifier are set by watching how this current responds.
notes.example: Watching the plate current meter dip as the tuning control is adjusted on a tube amplifier.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 6 (NAVEDTRA 14178), Glossary, “CONTROL GRID”

notes.front: What does the TUNE control do on a vacuum-tube RF power amplifier?
notes.back: Tunes the plate circuit to resonance; correctly set, it produces a pronounced dip in plate current.
notes.explanation: At resonance the tuned plate circuit draws the least plate current, so the meter shows a sharp dip, before the LOAD control sets the output.
notes.example: Like turning a radio dial until a station's signal peaks, except here the meter dips instead of rising.

notes.front: What does the LOAD (or COUPLING) control do on a vacuum-tube RF power amplifier?
notes.back: Sets the desired power output without exceeding the maximum allowable plate current.
notes.explanation: It is adjusted after TUNE, and by a different rule: output level and a current ceiling, not a dip.
notes.example: Like opening a tap to the flow you want, while watching a gauge so you never exceed its limit.

notes.front: What is “drive”, in the context of an RF power amplifier?
notes.back: The input signal level fed to the amplifier from the exciter or transceiver.
notes.explanation: Automatic level control exists specifically to stop drive from becoming excessive.
notes.example: Like the pressure feeding a pump: too much and the pump downstream is overdriven.

notes.front: What is a transmitter's keying line, to an external amplifier?
notes.back: The control signal that tells an external amplifier when to switch in and amplify.
notes.explanation: Delaying RF after this line activates gives the amplifier time to switch its antenna relay first.
notes.example: Keying an external amplifier's relay a few milliseconds before RF reaches it, so the antenna is already switched over.

notes.front: What is the dual-VFO feature on a transceiver commonly used for?
notes.back: To transmit on one frequency while listening on another.
notes.explanation: It is not full duplex or two simultaneous transmissions; only one VFO drives the transmitter at a time.
notes.example: A DX station transmits on 14.195 MHz and listens on 14.225 MHz: VFO A receives on 14.195 while VFO B transmits on 14.225.

notes.front: What is a receive attenuator for?
notes.back: To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals.
notes.explanation: It reduces the signal reaching the receiver's front end, before that signal can swamp it.
notes.example: Switching in 10 dB of attenuation so a nearby broadcast station no longer blocks reception of a weak signal.

notes.front: What is receiver overload?
notes.back: Distortion or blocking caused when a signal reaching the receiver's front end is too strong.
notes.explanation: A receive attenuator exists to prevent exactly this, by weakening the incoming signal first.
notes.example: Like a camera's picture washing out in direct sunlight until you fit a filter.

notes.front: What is an oscilloscope, and what makes it different from a voltmeter?
notes.back: A test instrument with horizontal and vertical amplifiers that displays complex waveforms, not just a single reading.
notes.explanation: A voltmeter gives one number; an oscilloscope draws the whole waveform shape over time.
notes.example: Like the difference between a speedometer's single number and a graph of speed over the whole journey.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 16 (NAVEDTRA 14188), ch. 6, “Use of the Oscilloscope”

notes.front: What is a keying waveform, and what is the best instrument for checking it on a CW transmitter?
notes.back: The shape of the on/off transmitted signal over time; an oscilloscope is the best instrument to check it.
notes.explanation: Only an instrument that draws the signal against time, like an oscilloscope, can show a waveform's shape.
notes.example: Like watching a light switch's dimming curve on a graph, not just whether it is on or off.

notes.front: What is a meter's input impedance?
notes.back: The impedance the meter itself presents to the circuit it is measuring.
notes.explanation: A high input impedance draws less current from the circuit under test, so it disturbs the reading less.
notes.example: A 10-megohm voltmeter draws almost no current from a high-impedance circuit it is measuring.

notes.front: What is meant by “loading” a circuit under test?
notes.back: Drawing enough current from a circuit while measuring it that the reading is disturbed.
notes.explanation: A voltmeter with high input impedance keeps its own loading small, so the circuit works almost as if it were not connected.
notes.example: A low-impedance meter across a high-impedance point pulls the voltage down as it measures it.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 16 (NAVEDTRA 14188), ch. 4, “Electronic Digital Multimeter”

notes.front: What is a digital multimeter's main advantage over an analog one?
notes.back: Higher precision in its readings.
notes.explanation: A numeric digital display resolves small differences that an analog needle cannot show as clearly.
notes.example: Like reading an exact number on a digital scale instead of judging a needle's position by eye.

notes.front: When is an analog multimeter preferred to a digital one?
notes.back: When adjusting a circuit for a maximum or minimum value.
notes.explanation: A moving needle shows the direction and speed of a change more naturally than a jumping digital number.
notes.example: Like watching a fuel gauge's needle swing rather than reading a digital number that keeps rounding.

notes.front: What signals are used to run a two-tone test?
notes.back: Two audio tones that are not harmonically related, fed into an SSB transmitter together.
notes.explanation: Neither tone is a harmonic of the other, so distortion products land on new frequencies where they are easy to see.
notes.example: Like playing two unrelated musical notes together and listening for any extra note that should not be there.

notes.front: What transmitter performance does a two-tone test analyse?
notes.back: Linearity: whether the amplifier reproduces the input signal shape without adding distortion.
notes.explanation: A two-tone test reveals non-linearity because any distortion product from the two tones exposes a departure from a straight input-output relationship.
notes.example: Like checking whether a photocopier reproduces a page at exactly the size and shape of the original.

notes.front: What does a notch filter reduce, specifically?
notes.explanation: It is aimed at unwanted steady carriers, not impulse noise or adjacent-channel splatter.
notes.back: Interference from carriers that fall inside the receiver passband.

notes.front: Why might you receive CW on the opposite (reverse) sideband?
notes.explanation: Switching sideband moves the receiver's effective listening slot, which can put an interferer outside the new passband.
notes.back: It may reduce or eliminate interference from other signals nearby.

notes.front: How does a noise blanker reduce impulse noise?
notes.explanation: It works in the time domain: gain drops only for the brief moment each pulse arrives.
notes.back: By reducing receiver gain during each noise pulse.

notes.front: What can happen if a receiver's noise reduction level is set too high?
notes.explanation: Noise reduction reshapes the audio continuously, so pushing it too far changes the wanted signal too.
notes.back: Received signals may become distorted.

notes.front: How are TUNE and LOAD set on a vacuum-tube RF power amplifier?
notes.explanation: The two controls use different signs of the same current reading: a dip to find resonance, then a ceiling to set output.
notes.back: TUNE for a pronounced dip in plate current; LOAD for the desired output without exceeding maximum plate current.

notes.front: Why is automatic level control (ALC) used with an RF power amplifier, and why should it be inactive on AFSK data?
notes.explanation: ALC works by reducing gain when drive rises, which is exactly the kind of gain change AFSK data signals cannot tolerate.
notes.back: ALC prevents excessive drive; on AFSK data, its action distorts the signal, so it should be inactive.

notes.front: What is the purpose of an antenna tuner?
notes.explanation: It matches the transmitter to the feed line at the rig end; it does not change the SWR on the feed line itself.
notes.back: To increase power transfer from the transmitter to the feed line.

notes.front: Why delay RF output after activating the keying line to an external amplifier?
notes.explanation: Without the delay, RF could reach the amplifier's antenna relay before it finishes switching.
notes.back: To give the amplifier time to switch the antenna between the transceiver and the amplifier output.

notes.front: What is the function of an electronic keyer?
notes.explanation: It is not a transmit/receive switch or a digital-mode interface; it only shapes CW timing.
notes.back: Automatic generation of dots and dashes for CW operation.

notes.front: What is a common use of the dual-VFO feature?
notes.explanation: It is not full duplex operation, and it does not transmit on two frequencies at once.
notes.back: To transmit on one frequency and listen on another.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a receive attenuator?
notes.explanation: It weakens the signal before the receiver's front end, rather than after distortion has already occurred.
notes.back: To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals.

notes.front: Why is an oscilloscope the right instrument for checking a CW keying waveform, and what signal feeds its vertical input for an RF envelope check?
notes.explanation: An oscilloscope contains horizontal and vertical channel amplifiers, letting it trace a signal's shape over time rather than give a single reading.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G4B01, G4B02, G4B03, G4B04
notes.back: It shows complex waveforms, unlike a voltmeter; the attenuated RF output of the transmitter feeds the vertical input.

notes.front: Why do voltmeters have high input impedance?
notes.explanation: A meter with high input impedance draws little current from the circuit, so the reading is closer to the circuit's true, undisturbed state.
notes.back: It decreases the loading on the circuit being measured.

notes.front: Digital or analog multimeter: which is better for higher precision, and which for adjusting a circuit to a maximum or minimum?
notes.explanation: A digital reading resolves small differences well, but a moving needle shows the trend of a changing value more naturally.
notes.back: Digital gives higher precision; analog is preferred when adjusting for a maximum or minimum value.

notes.front: What signals make up a two-tone test, and what does it measure?
notes.explanation: Neither tone is a harmonic of the other, so any distortion products land on new frequencies, revealing non-linear behaviour in the amplifier.
notes.back: Two non-harmonically related audio tones; the test measures linearity.

notes.front: What can a directional wattmeter be used to determine?
notes.explanation: By comparing forward and reflected power, it derives SWR rather than measuring it directly.
notes.back: Standing wave ratio (SWR).

notes.front: What must be connected to an antenna analyzer for SWR measurements, and what can strong nearby signals do to its readings?
notes.explanation: An antenna analyzer also measures the impedance of coaxial cable, but it needs the actual antenna system connected to give a meaningful SWR reading.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G4B11, G4B12, G4B13
notes.back: The antenna and feed line; strong nearby signals can interfere with the readings.

notes.front: What is the purpose of the notch filter found on many HF transceivers?
notes.back: To reduce interference from carriers in the receiver passband
notes.choices:
A) To restrict the transmitter voice bandwidth
B) To reduce interference from carriers in the receiver passband
C) To eliminate receiver interference from impulse noise sources
D) To remove interfering splatter generated by signals on adjacent frequencies
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is bandwidth restriction, not filtering. C: impulse noise is handled by a noise blanker. D: splatter from adjacent frequencies is a different problem from an in-band carrier.
notes.explanation: A notch filter cuts a narrow band to remove an unwanted steady carrier inside the passband.

notes.front: What is the benefit of using the opposite or “reverse” sideband when receiving CW?
notes.back: It may be possible to reduce or eliminate interference from other signals
notes.choices:
A) Interference from impulse noise will be eliminated
B) More stations can be accommodated within a given signal passband
C) It may be possible to reduce or eliminate interference from other signals
D) Accidental out-of-band operation can be prevented
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is unrelated to impulse noise. B: it does not add capacity to the passband. D: it has nothing to do with staying in-band.
notes.explanation: Listening on the reverse sideband shifts the receiver's effective slot, which can move an interferer out of it.

notes.front: How does a noise blanker work?
notes.back: By reducing receiver gain during a noise pulse
notes.choices:
A) By temporarily increasing received bandwidth
B) By redirecting noise pulses into a filter capacitor
C) By reducing receiver gain during a noise pulse
D) By clipping noise peaks
notes.choicesExplained: A: bandwidth is not changed. B: there is no capacitor redirection step. D: it does not clip peaks; it reduces gain.
notes.explanation: It only lowers gain for the brief moment each pulse occurs, then restores it.

notes.front: What is the effect on plate current of the correct setting of a vacuum-tube RF power amplifier’s TUNE control?
notes.back: A pronounced dip
notes.choices:
A) A pronounced peak
B) A pronounced dip
C) No change will be observed
D) A slow, rhythmic oscillation
notes.choicesExplained: A: the correct indication is a dip, not a peak. C: a real change should be observed. D: there is no oscillation involved.
notes.explanation: At resonance the tuned plate circuit draws the least plate current, so the meter shows a sharp dip.

notes.front: Why is automatic level control (ALC) used with an RF power amplifier?
notes.back: To prevent excessive drive
notes.choices:
A) To balance the transmitter audio frequency response
B) To reduce harmonic radiation
C) To prevent excessive drive
D) To increase overall efficiency
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not an audio equalizer. B: harmonic reduction is a filtering job, not ALC's. D: efficiency is not ALC's purpose.
notes.explanation: ALC reduces gain automatically when drive would otherwise become too high.

notes.front: What is the purpose of an antenna tuner?
notes.back: Increase power transfer from the transmitter to the feed line
notes.choices:
A) Reduce the SWR in the feed line to the antenna
B) Reduce the power dissipation in the feedline to the antenna
C) Increase power transfer from the transmitter to the feed line
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the feed line's own SWR is unchanged by a tuner at the transmitter. B: reducing dissipation is not its purpose. D: only C is correct, so “all these choices” is wrong.
notes.explanation: A tuner matches the transmitter to the feed line at the rig end; it does not change the SWR that already exists on the feed line itself.

notes.front: What happens as a receiver’s noise reduction control level is increased?
notes.back: Received signals may become distorted
notes.choices:
A) Received signals may become distorted
B) Received frequency may become unstable
C) CW signals may become severely attenuated
D) Received frequency may shift several kHz
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: frequency stability is not affected by noise reduction. C: CW is not specially attenuated by this control.
notes.explanation: Noise reduction reshapes the audio continuously, so pushing it too far distorts the wanted signal along with the noise.

notes.front: What is the correct adjustment for the LOAD or COUPLING control of a vacuum tube RF power amplifier?
notes.back: Desired power output without exceeding maximum allowable plate current
notes.choices:
A) Minimum SWR on the antenna
B) Minimum plate current without exceeding maximum allowable grid current
C) Highest plate voltage while minimizing grid current
D) Desired power output without exceeding maximum allowable plate current
notes.choicesExplained: A: SWR is not what LOAD controls. B and C: the limiting figure is plate current, not grid current or plate voltage.
notes.explanation: LOAD is set for output, not a current minimum, and the ceiling that matters is on plate current, not SWR or grid current.

notes.front: What is the purpose of delaying RF output after activating a transmitter’s keying line to an external amplifier?
notes.back: To allow time for the amplifier to switch the antenna between the transceiver and the amplifier output
notes.choices:
A) To prevent key clicks on CW
B) To prevent transient overmodulation
C) To allow time for the amplifier to switch the antenna between the transceiver and the amplifier output
D) To allow time for the amplifier power supply to reach operating level
notes.choicesExplained: A: key clicks are a shaping issue, not a switching delay. B: overmodulation is unrelated. D: the delay is only milliseconds, long enough for a relay but far too short for a power supply to come up.
notes.explanation: The delay lets the amplifier's antenna relay finish switching before RF actually arrives.

notes.front: What is the function of an electronic keyer?
notes.back: Automatic generation of dots and dashes for CW operation
notes.choices:
A) Automatic transmit/receive switching
B) Automatic generation of dots and dashes for CW operation
C) To allow time for switching the antenna from the receiver to the transmitter
D) Computer interface for PSK and RTTY operation
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is a separate T/R switching function. C: that describes an amplifier delay, not a keyer. D: PSK and RTTY use a different kind of interface.
notes.explanation: It shapes CW timing automatically from paddle or key input; it is not a T/R switch or a digital-mode interface.

notes.front: Why should the ALC system be inactive when transmitting AFSK data signals?
notes.back: The ALC action distorts the signal
notes.choices:
A) ALC will invert the modulation of the AFSK mode
B) The ALC action distorts the signal
C) When using digital modes, too much ALC activity can cause the transmitter to overheat
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: ALC does not invert modulation. C: overheating is not the stated reason. D: only B is correct.
notes.explanation: ALC's automatic gain changes are exactly the kind of disturbance AFSK data tones cannot tolerate.

notes.front: Which of the following is a common use of the dual-VFO feature on a transceiver?
notes.back: To transmit on one frequency and listen on another
notes.choices:
A) To allow transmitting on two frequencies at once
B) To permit full duplex operation -- that is, transmitting and receiving at the same time
C) To transmit on one frequency and listen on another
D) To improve frequency accuracy by allowing variable frequency output (VFO) operation
notes.choicesExplained: A: it does not transmit on two frequencies simultaneously. B: that describes full duplex, which this is not. D: frequency accuracy is not what dual VFO improves.
notes.explanation: Only one VFO drives the transmitter at a time; the other is used for listening.

notes.front: What is the purpose of using a receive attenuator?
notes.back: To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals
notes.choices:
A) To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals
B) To reduce the transmitter power when driving a linear amplifier
C) To reduce power consumption when operating from batteries
D) To reduce excessive audio level on strong signals
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not touch transmitter power. C: it is not a power-saving feature. D: it acts on RF, not on audio level.
notes.explanation: It weakens the signal ahead of the receiver's front end so strong signals cannot overload it.

notes.front: What item of test equipment contains horizontal and vertical channel amplifiers?
notes.back: An oscilloscope
notes.choices:
A) An ohmmeter
B) A signal generator
C) An ammeter
D) An oscilloscope
notes.choicesExplained: A, C: meters give a single reading, with no horizontal/vertical channels. B: a signal generator produces signals rather than displaying them.
notes.explanation: These two amplifier channels are what let an oscilloscope trace a waveform's shape over time.

notes.front: Which of the following is an advantage of an oscilloscope versus a digital voltmeter?
notes.back: Complex waveforms can be measured
notes.choices:
A) An oscilloscope uses less power
B) Complex impedances can be easily measured
C) Greater precision
D) Complex waveforms can be measured
notes.choicesExplained: A: power use is not the point of comparison. B: measuring complex impedance is not what an oscilloscope adds here. C: precision favours the digital voltmeter, not the scope.
notes.explanation: A digital voltmeter gives one precise number; an oscilloscope shows the whole waveform shape instead.

notes.front: Which of the following is the best instrument to use for checking the keying waveform of a CW transmitter?
notes.back: An oscilloscope
notes.choices:
A) An oscilloscope
B) A field strength meter
C) A sidetone monitor
D) A wavemeter
notes.choicesExplained: B: a field strength meter reads signal level, not waveform shape. C: a sidetone monitor is for the operator's ear, not for measurement. D: a wavemeter reads frequency, not waveform.
notes.explanation: Only an instrument that plots the signal against time can show a keying waveform's shape.

notes.front: What signal source is connected to the vertical input of an oscilloscope when checking the RF envelope pattern of a transmitted signal?
notes.back: The attenuated RF output of the transmitter
notes.choices:
A) The local oscillator of the transmitter
B) An external RF oscillator
C) The transmitter balanced mixer output
D) The attenuated RF output of the transmitter
notes.choicesExplained: A: the local oscillator does not carry the transmitted envelope. B: an external oscillator is unrelated to this transmitter's output. C: the mixer output alone is not the final transmitted envelope.
notes.explanation: The actual transmitted RF, reduced to a safe level, is what shows the real envelope shape.

notes.front: Why do voltmeters have high input impedance?
notes.back: It decreases the loading on circuits being measured
notes.choices:
A) It improves the frequency response
B) It allows for higher voltages to be safely measured
C) It improves the resolution of the readings
D) It decreases the loading on circuits being measured
notes.choicesExplained: A: frequency response is a separate design issue. B: high impedance is not about voltage safety limits. C: resolution is not directly improved by impedance alone.
notes.explanation: A high input impedance draws little current from the circuit, so the reading disturbs it less.

notes.front: What is an advantage of a digital multimeter as compared to an analog multimeter?
notes.back: Higher precision
notes.choices:
A) Better for measuring computer circuits
B) Less prone to overload
C) Higher precision
D) Faster response
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not specifically about computer circuits. B: overload tolerance is not the stated advantage. D: analog meters can respond faster to a changing value, not the digital one.
notes.explanation: A numeric digital display resolves finer differences than an analog needle can show.

notes.front: What signals are used to conduct a two-tone test?
notes.back: Two non-harmonically related audio signals
notes.choices:
A) Two audio signals of the same frequency shifted 90 degrees
B) Two non-harmonically related audio signals
C) Two swept frequency tones
D) Two audio frequency range square wave signals of equal amplitude
notes.choicesExplained: A: a 90-degree phase shift describes an I-Q pair, not a two-tone test. C: the tones are fixed, not swept. D: they are not square waves.
notes.explanation: Because the tones share no common overtones, any extra tones at the output must be distortion products.

notes.front: What transmitter performance parameter does a two-tone test analyze?
notes.back: Linearity
notes.choices:
A) Linearity
B) Percentage of suppression of the carrier and undesired sideband for SSB
C) Percentage of frequency modulation
D) Percentage of carrier phase shift
notes.choicesExplained: B: carrier and sideband suppression are checked by other means, not a two-tone test. C: frequency modulation percentage is unrelated to SSB linearity testing. D: phase shift is not what this test measures.
notes.explanation: Distortion products from the two unrelated tones reveal non-linear behaviour in the amplifier.

notes.front: When is an analog multimeter preferred to a digital multimeter?
notes.back: When adjusting circuits for maximum or minimum values
notes.choices:
A) When testing logic circuits
B) When high precision is desired
C) When measuring the frequency of an oscillator
D) When adjusting circuits for maximum or minimum values
notes.choicesExplained: A: logic circuits are not the stated reason. B: precision favours digital, not analog. C: frequency is better measured with a dedicated frequency counter.
notes.explanation: A moving needle shows the trend of a changing value more naturally than a digital display's jumping numbers.

notes.front: Which of the following can be determined with a directional wattmeter?
notes.back: Standing wave ratio
notes.choices:
A) Standing wave ratio
B) Antenna front-to-back ratio
C) RF interference
D) Radio wave propagation
notes.choicesExplained: B: front-to-back ratio needs a pattern measurement, not a wattmeter. C and D: interference and propagation are not what a directional wattmeter measures.
notes.explanation: By comparing forward and reflected power it lets you derive SWR.

notes.front: Which of the following must be connected to an antenna analyzer when it is being used for SWR measurements?
notes.back: Antenna and feed line
notes.choices:
A) Receiver
B) Transmitter
C) Antenna and feed line
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: neither the receiver nor the transmitter is needed; the analyzer supplies its own signal. D: since only C is correct, “all these choices” is wrong.
notes.explanation: An analyzer supplies its own low-power test signal, so it needs only the antenna system connected, not the station's receiver or transmitter.

notes.front: What effect can strong signals from nearby transmitters have on an antenna analyzer?
notes.back: Received power that interferes with SWR readings
notes.choices:
A) Desensitization which can cause intermodulation products which interfere with impedance readings
B) Received power that interferes with SWR readings
C) Generation of harmonics which interfere with frequency readings
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the strong signal simply adds received power to the analyzer's own weak test signal; the pool does not treat it as desensitization or intermodulation. C: harmonic generation is not the stated effect. D: only B is correct.
notes.explanation: A strong nearby signal picked up through the antenna can disturb the analyzer's own low-level measurement.

notes.front: Which of the following can be measured with an antenna analyzer?
notes.back: Impedance of coaxial cable
notes.choices:
A) Front-to-back ratio of an antenna
B) Power output from a transmitter
C) Impedance of coaxial cable
D) Gain of a directional antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: front-to-back ratio and gain need a full pattern measurement, not just an analyzer. B: transmitter power output is a wattmeter's job.
notes.explanation: An antenna analyzer measures impedance directly; front-to-back ratio and gain need a pattern test, and transmitter power needs a wattmeter.

notes.front: Notch filter, noise blanker or noise reduction: which removes an in-band carrier, and which acts only during noise pulses?
notes.back: A notch filter removes an in-band carrier; a noise blanker cuts gain only during each noise pulse; noise reduction shapes audio continuously.
notes.explanation: Each acts on a different kind of interference: a steady carrier, a brief pulse, or general background noise.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G4A01, G4A03, G4A07

notes.front: TUNE or LOAD control: which is set for a pronounced dip in plate current, and which for desired output within a plate-current limit?
notes.back: TUNE is set for a pronounced dip in plate current; LOAD is set for the desired output without exceeding maximum plate current.
notes.explanation: TUNE finds resonance first, shown as a dip; LOAD then sets how much output that resonant circuit delivers.

notes.front: Digital or analog multimeter: which gives higher precision, and which is better for adjusting a circuit to a maximum or minimum?
notes.back: Digital gives higher precision; analog is better for adjusting to a maximum or minimum, because its needle shows a trend.
notes.explanation: A number is exact but static from reading to reading; a needle's motion shows which way, and how fast, a value is changing.
